ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 3 — Annual Wellness Visit, Subsequent — Johnny Cash

text.paragraph: Subsequent annual wellness visit; no new complaints. [S]

Mr. Cash is a 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes complicated by autonomic and peripheral neuropathy, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, and severe primary open-angle glaucoma, who returns for his subsequent annual wellness visit four weeks after his endocrinology consultation. Sitagliptin and low-dose midodrine were started then. He completed the health risk assessment before the visit, with a family member reading the questions aloud because of his low vision. He stands up in stages, sleeps with the head of the bed raised, and wears waist-high compression; the lightheadedness on standing is less frequent, and he has had no falls since the consultation. His home glucose readings show no values below 70 mg/dL. He uses both eye drops as prescribed and has added no over-the-counter medicines. He is recording at home and writing most days. [S]

list.item:
Subsequent annual wellness visit completed. Health risk assessment reviewed, personalized prevention plan updated, and a large-print copy given. Depression and alcohol screens are negative. Cognition is normal by direct observation, and the Mini-Cog at the first visit two months ago was 5 of 5, so it was not repeated. Fall risk is high. [S]
Next annual wellness visit in one year.

Type 2 diabetes with diabetic autonomic neuropathy (E11.43). HbA1c 8.6% at the first visit, above his individualized goal below 7.5%. Home readings have improved since sitagliptin was added, with no hypoglycemia. Kidney screening is current: urine albumin-creatinine ratio 18 mg/g and eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73 m², both normal. [S]
Continue metformin 1000 mg twice daily and sitagliptin 100 mg daily.
HbA1c and lipids at the three-month review in about five weeks; urine albumin-creatinine ratio and eGFR yearly.

Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (I95.1). Standing systolic pressure 116 mmHg, up from 112 mmHg at the first visit, on midodrine 2.5 mg three times daily. Still mildly symptomatic. [S]
Continue midodrine with the last dose at least four hours before bed, staged standing, head-of-bed elevation, compression, and 2 liters of fluid a day.
Review the dose at the three-month visit, with a supine blood pressure check.

Diabetic peripheral neuropathy with loss of protective sensation (E11.42). Foot examination today shows no ulcer or pre-ulcerative lesion; sensory loss unchanged. [S]
Daily self-inspection with a family member's help because of his vision.
Continue protective footwear; foot examination at every visit.

Primary open-angle glaucoma, severe stage (H40.1133). Eye pressures were above target at the first visit, and dorzolamide was added to latanoprost. The dilated eye examination two months ago also covered diabetic retinopathy screening. Neither drop lowers blood pressure or heart rate. [S]
Continue latanoprost and dorzolamide.
Eye pressure check at the three-month review; OCT and visual fields at six months with the eye clinic.

High fall risk. Orthostatic hypotension, loss of foot sensation, leg weakness, low vision, and earlier falls. Timed Up and Go 14 seconds with a cane. [S]
Refer to physical therapy for gait, strength, and balance training.
Refer to low-vision rehabilitation for a home lighting and safety review, including a second stair handrail.

Follow-up: Physical therapy and low-vision rehabilitation referrals placed. Return the FIT kit by mail. Three-month diabetes, blood pressure, and eye pressure review in about five weeks, with HbA1c, lipids, hepatitis C screening, and the first zoster dose. Next annual wellness visit in one year. Next scheduled visit 2026-05-29: three-month diabetes, blood pressure, and eye pressure review. [S]

Voluntary advance care planning discussion of about 20 minutes, with his consent. He has a written health care directive and has named a health care agent; a copy is now in the chart. He described what matters most to him: keeping the sight he has left, staying at home, and continuing to write and record. The discussion covered how to make his wishes known if he could not speak for himself and how to keep the directive with his agent. He will review his wishes with his agent and revisit them at a future visit. [S]
